<reason>Side A (PRO) built the cleaner comparative case: enforcement leaves labor demand intact and only reprices/relocates flows (Hungary reroute, Aegean-to-Libya shift, circular migration freezing into permanent settlement), while each permit subtracts a crossing. A's challenge to name a land border where enforcement cut total flows put sustained pressure on B, and B's Balkan-corridor answer was partly deflected by attributing the 2016 drop to the Turkey deal. A answered B's best pressure (the displacement double standard) with the subtraction-vs-relocation asymmetry, and neutralized the scale critique with Bracero, which B never squarely rebutted, and the 1986 magnet with the amnesty-vs-prospective-permit distinction. B's strongest live routes—compliance depends on enforcement scaffolding, and pathways "manufacture applicants"—were original and memorable but ultimately rested on asserted mechanisms A at least contested on coherent grounds. A's clipped Rebuttal 2 is a real execution cost, but its substance was mostly delivered. B was highly competent and rhetorically sharp, but A controlled the decisive clash and made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The displacement double-standard exchange: B's Q2 forced A to explain why route-shifting discredits enforcement but not pathways; A's Rebuttal 2 answer—that enforcement displacement grows with scale while pathway displacement shrinks, because each permit removes a crossing rather than relocating it—was the debate's most decisive move, and B's "manufactures an applicant" rejoinder in the closing kept it contested but did not fully neutralize it.</best_rebuttal>
